ON-CALL AND STANDBY TIME COMPENSABILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this On-Call and Standby Time information sheet to describe how California wage law approaches time that Jordan Lee or another employee spends on call or on standby — that is, time before the employee has been called in or has otherwise reported for work. California's wage orders define "hours worked" using a control-based test, and courts have applied that test to determine whether on-call or standby time itself counts as compensable hours worked. This document addresses that question and is separate from this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet, which addresses the narrower situation of an employee who has already reported to work and is then not put to work, or is furnished less than half the usual scheduled day.

THE GENERAL "HOURS WORKED" DEFINITION: SUBJECT TO EMPLOYER CONTROL
Under the applicable California IWC Wage Order, "hours worked" means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so. This control-based definition is not limited to time an employee spends actively performing tasks; it turns on the degree to which the employer controls how Jordan Lee may use the time in question, including time before Jordan Lee has been called in to perform any specific task.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Hours worked” means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(L), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is a single regulatory subdivision within IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the same catch-all wage order this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet and other during-employment documents already verify. It was fetched directly from the Department of Industrial Relations at https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf, which was reachable in this session and was fetched twice with two distinct User-Agent strings, producing byte-identical files (confirmed by checksum). The "subject to control" language is a long-standing, frequently-quoted definition, but this session did not independently confirm whether its wording has changed since Wage Order 4-2001's original adoption — the fetched PDF reflects the wage order's currently operative text, which includes minimum wage figures effective through January 1, 2026, well after 2001. Other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for public housekeeping or Wage Order 7 for mercantile employees) contain an hours-worked definition in the same numbered subdivision with materially the same "subject to control" formula, but those other orders were not independently fetched or checked in this session — this clause verifies Wage Order 4-2001 only. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California provides — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law, or which industry's wage order, governs a specific employment relationship.

A DIFFERENT "HOURS WORKED" STANDARD FOR THE HEALTH CARE INDUSTRY
The same wage order provision states a separate definition of "hours worked" for employees in the health care industry: for those employees, "hours worked" means the time during which the employee is suffered or permitted to work for the employer, whether or not required to do so, as interpreted in accordance with the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act — a formulation that does not repeat the general definition's "subject to the control of an employer" language.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Within the health care industry, the term “hours worked” means the time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work for the employer, whether or not"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(L), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "required to do so, as interpreted in accordance with the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(L), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is the same regulatory subdivision as the general hours-worked definition cited elsewhere in this document (§ 2(L)) — not an independent source, but a second sentence within it describing a narrower, industry-specific standard. In the source PDF, a footnote about minimum-wage rate adjustments is inserted mid-sentence at a page break, which is why this clause's citations are split into two separately-quoted fragments rather than one continuous quote; nothing was omitted between them beyond that footnote's own text, and each fragment quoted below is independently an exact, contiguous substring of the fetched text. The wage order incorporates federal Fair Labor Standards Act interpretive standards by reference for health-care-industry employees but does not itself state what those federal interpretive standards say about on-call time, and this document does not independently research or summarize federal FLSA on-call case law. "Employees in the health care industry" is itself a separately defined term in this same wage order (§ 2(H)); this document does not independently verify which employees fall within that definition. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

JUDICIALLY DEVELOPED FACTORS FOR APPLYING THE CONTROL TEST TO ON-CALL AND STANDBY TIME
California courts have applied the wage order's control-based "hours worked" definition to on-call and standby arrangements in decisions addressing a range of industries and on-call structures. In doing so, this body of case law has generally examined a set of practical factors bearing on how much control an employer retains over an employee's own time during an on-call or standby period, including: the extent of any geographic restriction on where the employee may go while on call; how much advance notice or response time the employee is given before being required to report or begin working if called; whether the on-call arrangement leaves the employee free to engage in personal activities during the on-call period; and how frequently the employee is actually called in to work during on-call periods. Courts applying these factors have generally treated the inquiry as one of degree, weighing the factors together against the wage order's control-based definition rather than treating any single factor as automatically dispositive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Hours worked” means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(L), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause describes considerations that recur in this area of California case law only in general terms; it does not cite, quote, or rely on any specific court decision for the factor list itself, and that description should be read as a general, unverified summary of the doctrine rather than a confirmed holding of any case. This corpus's verification discipline calls for independently confirming case law through CourtListener before citing it. Before drafting this document, a single lightweight CourtListener search call was made to check whether the daily request quota was available; it returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response reporting that CourtListener's daily request cap (125 requests/day) had already been exhausted by earlier research in this same session, with the next availability approximately 5.7 hours out (server-reported: 20,464 seconds) at the time of the attempt. Rather than waiting out that rate limit or presenting an unverified case citation as verified, this document proceeds on a statute/regulation-only basis for this point: it does not cite Mendiola v. CPS Security Solutions, Inc. (2015) 60 Cal.4th 833 — a California Supreme Court decision commonly associated with on-call/standby compensability, addressing on-call sleep time for security guards — or any other specific case, because this session did not independently verify that or any other case's actual holding against its opinion text. The only source cited for this clause is the wage order's own control-based definition, quoted elsewhere in this document and reused here as the anchor text this body of case law interprets; the factor list is offered as a general description of a well-developed area of law, not as a verified quotation from, or holding of, any specific opinion.

"HOURS WORKED" CLASSIFICATION GOVERNS MINIMUM WAGE AND OVERTIME CALCULATIONS
Time that qualifies as "hours worked" under the definition described above is counted for purposes of California's minimum wage and overtime requirements in the same way as any other work time. The wage order requires that every employer pay each employee not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, regardless of whether wages are measured by time, piece, commission, or another method, and separately requires overtime compensation once hours worked in a workday or workweek exceed specified thresholds. This document does not determine, for any particular on-call or standby arrangement involving Jordan Lee, whether that time in fact meets the "hours worked" definition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(B), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(B) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "Such employees shall not be employed more than eight (8) hours in any workday or more than 40 hours in any workweek unless the employee receives one and one- half ( 1½) times such employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over 40 hours in the workweek."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(A)(1), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(A)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: Section 4(B) (minimum wage) and Section 3(A)(1) (daily/weekly overtime) are separate, independently numbered subdivisions of the same wage order already cited elsewhere in this document for the hours-worked definition, and, in this corpus's existing Reporting Time Pay information sheet, for reporting time pay — they are cited here for the narrower point that both the minimum-wage and overtime provisions operate on whatever time counts as "hours worked," not as independent corroboration of each other. This clause states a structural relationship between provisions; it does not calculate, and does not purport to calculate, wages owed for any actual on-call or standby period, and it does not resolve whether any particular period is "hours worked" in the first place — that threshold determination is the subject of the definition and factors described elsewhere in this document. The overtime quotation below reflects a minor internal spacing irregularity ("one and one- half ( 1½)") present in the source PDF's own text extraction; it is quoted exactly as extracted. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

HOW THIS DOCUMENT DIFFERS FROM REPORTING TIME PAY
The same wage order's reporting-time-pay provisions include a separate, narrower carve-out: they do not apply to an employee on paid standby status who is called to perform assigned work at a time other than the employee's scheduled reporting time. That carve-out concerns whether the reporting-time-pay formula — which is triggered when an employee is required to report for work and does report — applies to a standby employee's later call-in. It does not address, and does not answer, the separate and broader question addressed in this document: whether time spent on call or on standby, before any call-in occurs, itself counts as compensable "hours worked" under the control-based definition described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section shall not apply to an employee on paid standby status who is called to perform assigned work at a time other than the employee’s scheduled reporting time."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(D), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause cites the same wage order subdivision (§ 5(D)) already quoted in this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet (clause reportingtime_exceptions); it is independently re-verified here from a separate fetch of the same source PDF made in this session, for this document's distinct interpretive point about scope, not as a new or different source. This document does not restate the Reporting Time Pay information sheet's core rule, second-reporting rule, or its other exceptions; readers are directed to that existing document for the requirements it covers. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.
